title: Enolates: the α-carbon attacks
review: Step 1 shows the acetone enolate drawn as the C=C–O⁻ resonance form with the α-carbon lit as the nucleophile. Step 3 says ester enolate + ester forms a β-keto ester 'kicking out EtO⁻'; step 9 treats 2-methylcyclohexanone + LDA at −78 °C as deprotonating C6 (the CH2 side). Please confirm the wording of the kinetic/thermodynamic explanation.

steps.text: A base removes an **α-H**, the H on the carbon next to a C=O. The enolate that forms reacts through that α-carbon, so it is a carbon nucleophile. It then runs a pattern you know: A on an aldehyde or ketone (aldol), B on an ester (Claisen), C on an enone (Michael), or SN2 on an alkyl halide (alkylation).
Pentan-3-one plus base. Tap an **α-carbon** the base can deprotonate.
steps.explain: The α-carbons are the two CH2 groups right next to C=O (they are equivalent here). Their C–H is acidic because the negative charge left behind spreads onto the oxygen. The CH3 groups at the ends are β, not α.

steps.text: An enolate is mixed with CH3I. Which kind of reaction is that?

options.text: SN2: the α-carbon attacks CH3 and pushes out I⁻ (alkylation)
options.explains: CH3I has no C=O; it is a methyl halide, the best SN2 substrate. The enolate is just the nucleophile.

options.text: Pattern A: addition to a C=O
options.explains: Pattern A needs an aldehyde or ketone C=O to add to. CH3I has none.

options.text: Pattern B: acyl substitution, because I⁻ leaves
options.explains: A leaving group alone isn't pattern B; that needs a C=O carbon carrying the leaving group (an acid derivative). Here I⁻ leaves from an sp³ carbon: SN2.
Pattern C needs a C=C next to a C=O (an enone). CH3I has neither.

steps.text: Enolate + pattern A. The O⁻ pushes down, the α-carbon attacks the other aldehyde's C=O, and those π electrons go onto O.
Same key step with propanal. The first arrow (O⁻ pushing down) is drawn; add the other two.
Aldol gives a β-hydroxy carbonyl, but Claisen gives a β-keto ester. **Why** the difference?

options.text: In Claisen the enolate adds to an ester, whose C=O carbon has a leaving group (EtO⁻), so the intermediate collapses back to C=O. An aldehyde has no leaving group, so the alkoxide is just protonated.
options.explains: Right: aldol = enolate + pattern A, Claisen = enolate + pattern B.

options.text: Claisen uses ethoxide and aldol uses hydroxide; the base decides the product.
options.explains: The base only makes the enolate (NaOEt is used with ethyl esters to avoid swapping the ester group). What happens after attack depends on the electrophile.

options.text: In Claisen the β-hydroxy ester forms first and is then oxidised to the ketone.
options.explains: No oxidant is present. The C=O re-forms because EtO⁻ leaves, not by oxidation.

options.text: In Claisen the alkoxide loses water, as in aldol condensation.
options.explains: Losing water (E1cB) makes a C=C, not a C=O. The ketone in the Claisen product comes from losing EtO⁻.

steps.text: **Kinetic vs thermodynamic.** LDA is a strong, bulky base, and at −78 °C it removes a proton fast and for good. On 2-methylcyclohexanone, tap the α-carbon LDA deprotonates.
steps.explain: LDA takes the most accessible H, on the CH2 side (C6). That gives the less substituted, kinetic enolate. A weaker base at room temperature deprotonates reversibly, so it ends up at the more substituted, more stable thermodynamic enolate on C2, the carbon with the methyl.
